markingScheme.criterion: Accurately describes the observed relationship between salinity and buoyancy, quoting at least one low-salinity and one high-salinity trial (density reading and egg result) from their own Investigation Record.
markingScheme.accept: Any two genuine trials from the student's own record showing the egg sinking at lower salinity/density and floating at higher salinity/density; exact numbers do not need to match a 'model' pair.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating 'the egg floated more' with no actual density/salinity figures quoted from their own trials.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that increasing dissolved salt increases the density of the water, and therefore increases the buoyant (upward) force on the egg.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent scientific wording (e.g. 'denser water pushes up harder', 'more concentrated water supports more weight'); do not require the exact phrase 'buoyant force' when the meaning is clearly density → greater upward force.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying salt 'makes the egg float' without linking it to density or an upward force — this restates the observation rather than explaining it.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly states whether the hypothesis (from Predict) was supported, and links this judgement explicitly to their own investigation evidence.
markingScheme.accept: Any judgement (supported / not supported / partially supported) that is consistent with what their own data actually shows and refers back to it.
markingScheme.insufficient: Repeating the hypothesis wording without saying whether the evidence agreed with it.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly compares the salinity of the Dead Sea (about 34%) and ordinary ocean water (about 3.5%), naming both bodies of water.
markingScheme.accept: Approximate figures are fine (e.g. 'around 30%+' vs 'around 3-4%') as long as the direction and rough scale of the difference is correct.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that the Dead Sea's higher salinity increases the density of its water.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent scientific wording (e.g. 'more dissolved salt makes the water heavier for its size', 'more concentrated water'); do not require the exact word 'density' if the meaning is clearly present.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating only 'the Dead Sea is saltier' with no mention of density.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that the greater density creates a greater buoyant (upward) force, so the swimmer needs less effort to remain afloat.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent wording for the mechanism, as in the Explain question (e.g. 'the water pushes up on them harder', 'they don't have to work as hard to stay up'); the word 'buoyant' itself is not required if the upward-force-and-reduced-effort idea is clearly present.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating that the water is 'denser' without going on to connect that to buoyant force and reduced swimming effort.

criteria.source: Auto-marked from the Knowledge Check (auto_marked_score, kc1-kc4) — the teacher does not mark this row.

= the Explain question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (own-investigation evidence, density/buoyancy mechanism, hypothesis judgement). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here. Every level below restates the same three analytic points as bands — never a different route to the same score.

levels.descriptor: No relevant low- or high-salinity evidence quoted from their own investigation, no density/buoyancy mechanism explained, and no judgement made about whether the hypothesis was supported.

Achieves only ONE of the three: quotes relevant evidence from their own Investigation Record OR explains the density/buoyancy mechanism OR states whether the hypothesis was supported — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. quotes relevant low- and high-salinity evidence and explains the density/buoyancy mechanism, but does not go on to judge the hypothesis against that evidence (or reaches a judgement using the evidence but the mechanism explanation is missing or wrong).

Uses relevant low- and high-salinity evidence from their own investigation, explains the density/buoyancy mechanism correctly, and states whether the hypothesis was supported using that evidence — all three analytic points present.

criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (salinity comparison, density mechanism, buoyancy/effort application). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here. Every level below restates the same three analytic points as bands — never a different route to the same score.

levels.descriptor: No valid comparison of the Dead Sea's and ordinary ocean's salinity, no density mechanism explained, and no application to why the swimmer needs less effort to float.

Achieves only ONE of the three: compares the two seas' salinity OR explains that higher salinity increases density OR explains the resulting reduction in swimming effort — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. compares salinity and explains the density mechanism, but does not go on to explain the effect on the swimmer's effort (or compares salinity and explains the reduced-effort outcome but skips the density step).

Compares the salinity of the Dead Sea and the ordinary ocean, explains that higher salinity increases water density, and explains that the resulting greater buoyant force means the swimmer needs less effort to remain afloat — all three analytic points present.

criteria.source: Assessed holistically across BOTH the Explain and Apply answers together — independent of, and never overlapping with, the content marks in use_of_evidence and reasoning above.

levels.descriptor: Hard to follow, or key vocabulary is missing/incorrect.
Understandable, but with unclear phrasing or a missing/misused term.
Clear, full sentences across both answers using correct terms such as salinity, density, buoyant force, hydrometer.

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Both questions reward three linked steps, not independent 'reasons' — award marks point-by-point using each question's marking_scheme in marking_context: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain marking_scheme's 3 points (own-investigation evidence, density/buoyancy mechanism, hypothesis judgement), and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply marking_scheme's 3 points (salinity comparison, density mechanism, buoyancy/effort application) — the rubric levels restate the exact same three points as bands at every mark value, never a different route to the same score; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. The Knowledge Check is already auto-marked in auto_marked_score — copy it into knowledge_accuracy (7 marks = full). Use the student's actual logged trials (the salinity/density/egg/buoyancy columns in simulation_results.trials) to verify any reading they claim to quote — do not take their prose summary on trust if it does not match their own logged data. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording per each point's 'accept' field, and do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 15 (7 auto + 3 + 3 + 2); report the percentage, one strength, one correction, and one next step, in under 80 words.
